title: NCLB Wasn't Perfect, but Abandoning Accountability Was Worse
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman responds to a New York Times op-ed by Ross Wiener that argues against restoring NCLB-style accountability, and makes the counter-case that the No Child Left Behind era coincided with some of the strongest achievement gains in recent American education history — particularly for Black, Hispanic, low-income students, and students with disabilities. Aldeman is particularly critical of Wiener's pivot from believing in objective measures to arguing that the pursuit of test scores caused harm, calling it incurious about why achievement rose under NCLB and fell sharply after it was replaced. The article contests the framing that test-based accountability and rich educational experiences are inherently in tension, arguing that foundational literacy and math are the enabling condition for project-based learning, civic engagement, and other goals — not their enemies. Aldeman also challenges the broader trend of schools reporting higher graduation rates and better grades while objective measures show students learning less, describing this as 'comforting stories' that objective accountability systems were designed to interrupt.
points: The NCLB era (2002-2015) coincided with some of the fastest achievement gains on record for the most disadvantaged students — Black, Hispanic, low-income, students with disabilities, and English Learners — and when it ended, those gains reversed sharply, particularly for the lowest performers.

Wiener's op-ed implies a tradeoff between reading/math achievement and richer educational experiences, but Aldeman argues there is no inherent tradeoff: solid foundational skills in literacy and math are what make project-based learning, civic engagement, and meaningful education possible.

Without objective, comparable accountability data, schools can tell comforting stories indefinitely — and the rise in grade inflation and higher graduation rates alongside declining objective measures is exactly the consequence the original accountability systems were designed to prevent.

The argument that objective standardized measures caused harm by being taken too seriously is, for Aldeman, a hard pivot from the pre-NCLB consensus that poor and minority students' low performance was invisible and unacknowledged — and therefore unchallenged.

Over 40 states have already enacted science-of-reading reforms independently, which raises Aldeman's fundamental question about the proposed READ Act: what is the case for federal intervention to lead a parade that states are already in?
quotes: Ross Wiener's op-ed struck me as oddly incurious about why achievement scores rose during the No Child Left Behind era and why scores declined when it ended.

Before NCLB, many states simply did not know — or did not publicly acknowledge — how poorly some groups of students were performing. Without objective, comparable data, schools can tell comforting stories indefinitely.

There's no inherent tradeoff. A school can (and should): teach kids to read and do math fluently, build strong character, offer meaningful projects, foster civic engagement, and create a welcoming environment so kids want to come to school. These things are not in tension.

Solid fundamental skills in literacy and math are often what makes many of the other goals possible. Students who struggle with the basics are less able to participate in project-based learning, civic engagement, career preparation, and almost every other educational aspiration.

When NCLB was no longer in effect, achievement scores fell, and they fell particularly fast for the lowest performing students. Now, is this just a coincidence? Maybe? But school accountability policy could plausibly explain at least some portion of what we're seeing.
Over 40 states have enacted science-of-reading reforms already; what's the case for Uncle Sam trying to jump out and lead this parade?
